title: How CEOs Should Think About AI - Insights From 3 Tech-Savvy Leaders
text:
Most CEOs I speak with are under extreme pressure from their boards to apply advanced AI in their businesses. It’s no secret that AI has enormous potential and power, yet while AI has been around for decades we are still really in the infancy stages, with rapid evolution. To understand at a deeper level how CEOs should view AI, I asked leaders from Broadcom, Google Fiber, and Calix. They shared three fundamentals CEOs should consider:
1. UNDERSTAND THE RAG MODEL
Right now, AI is still transactional. However, we have already seen shifts indicating AI is becoming experiential. Everyone is talking about generative AI, but what CEOs need to understand is a new variation called the RAG Model, which stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. This framework combines traditional databases with generative large language models. Michael Weening, CEO, Calix discussed how this accelerates outcomes for CEOs by mitigating one of the biggest obstacles associated with generative AI.
“These sophisticated systems, which are trained on data from the internet, have been known to provide answers that are unjustified and just plain wrong,” Weening said. “RAG architectures help prevent hallucinations by combining a large language model with business-specific data sources — think databases and documents. This integration helps ensure the AI is operating on the latest, most accurate data and that users can check sources for accuracy — two crucial requirements. CEOs are generally worried by Gen AI, but RAG architectures make it ready for business.”
2. DO NOT EXPECT MIRACLES FROM AI OVERNIGHT
There are so many advances in AI that many applications almost seem like you’re waving a magic wand. For those — like many CEOs — who are not living in the advanced AI world and instead doing their job of running an enterprise, they can be thrown new ideas and use cases which seem relevant. According to John Keib, Chief Technology and Product Officer, GFiber (Google) CEOs need to challenge themselves.
“They need to be able to think of things that they could never do before – exponentially,” Keib said. “It’s about moving from transactional AI to experiential AI, taking disparate data sets and combining them into an outcome, which has a lot more value.”
3. LOCATE THE VALUE
CEOs have learned not to follow the shiny object, and most will not just use technology for technology’s sake – no matter how exciting it is. After interviewing over 1,000 top CEOs, I can say a CEO’s job can be summed up in just six words: “To get from here to there.” And getting there is usually about creating new value that didn’t exist before. Charlie Kawwas, President, Semiconductor Solutions Group, Broadcom cited the potential of AI to provide consumers with better cybersecurity protection.
“Customers would be excited,” Kawwas said. “Because we would be protecting grandma, protecting kids, protecting families. And people would pay more to get a service like that.”
In Summary, the changes AI will usher in will have profound impact on business the economy and society. CEOs can leapfrog competitors and accelerate progress with the right focus ... and perspective.

title: Author Post: Harnessing AI to Bridge Health Equity: A Call to Action
text:
In today’s rapidly advancing healthcare landscape, artificial intelligence (AI) is at the forefront of innovation, especially in the realm of Clinical Decision Support (CDS) systems. These systems have the potential to revolutionize healthcare by providing clinicians with invaluable insights, from suggesting preventive measures to making accurate diagnoses.
However, as we embrace this transformative technology, we must address the inequities inherent within these AI systems that risk exacerbating existing health disparities. It is imperative that we ensure AI serves as a tool for equitable access and quality care for all, not just a privileged few.
The Promise and Perils of AI in Healthcare
AI in healthcare promises significant benefits, including improved diagnostic accuracy, personalized treatment plans, and enhanced operational efficiencies. Yet, this technology is not without its challenges. AI systems, particularly those used in CDS, are only as good as the data they are trained on. If these datasets reflect societal biases, the resulting algorithms will inevitably perpetuate these biases, thereby widening the gap in healthcare delivery.
As part of their efforts and outreach to Congress, per helping to shape policy around AI, the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) recently wrote an article on the urgency of this issue. The report underscores how population health management algorithms, which often proxy healthcare needs with costs, can allocate more care to white patients than to Black patients, even when health needs are equivalent.
This disparity arises because the algorithms tend to favor frequent users of healthcare services, who are disproportionately white due to existing inequities in healthcare access. A causal factor of this is that black patients tend to use less healthcare than white patients, in part due to inequities impacting healthcare access.
Moreover, the financial impact of health disparities is staggering. According to the FAS, these disparities contribute to an estimated $320 billion in excess healthcare spending annually. Without intervention, this figure is projected to increase to $1 trillion by 2040. These statistics underscore the critical need for immediate action to address biases in AI systems.
Legislative and Regulatory Action
Governments and organizations are beginning to recognize the need for equitable AI in healthcare. The White House has announced substantial investments, including $140 million for the National Science Foundation (NSF) to establish institutes dedicated to assessing existing generative AI (GenAI) systems. While these investments are a step in the right direction, more comprehensive measures are needed to ensure that AI systems are developed and deployed in a manner that promotes fairness and equity.
One of the key legislative efforts in this regard is President Biden's blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights. This initiative aims to protect individuals from potential harms associated with AI by establishing principles to guide its design, use, and deployment. Furthermore, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has released a beta version of its regulatory framework for medical device AI used in healthcare, and the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) has proposed revisions to Section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act to explicitly prohibit discrimination in the use of clinical algorithms.
Key Actions for Equitable AI
To harness the full potential of AI in healthcare while ensuring equity, we must focus on several key areas:
- Legislation and Standards: Policymakers must establish stringent AI governance, auditing, and transparency standards. This includes rigorous pre-deployment evaluations to test for biases and ensure data privacy. Regular audits should be mandated to verify ongoing compliance and adapt to evolving standards. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is well-positioned to lead these efforts, given that nearly 40% of Americans receive benefits under a Medicare or Medicaid program.
- Investment in Accessibility: Allocating funds to ensure AI accessibility for underserved populations is essential. The federal government should provide subsidies to AI service providers that support safety-net and rural health providers. Strategic innovation funding should be directed towards federally qualified health centers and rural health providers to contribute to and consume equitable AI.
- Diverse Data Collection: Promoting comprehensive data collection and collaboration among healthcare entities is crucial. AI models must be trained on diverse datasets to avoid homogeneity and biases. The government should incentivize healthcare organizations to share anonymized patient data for research purposes while ensuring patient privacy and data security. Increased reimbursement from CMS for particular services or conditions that involve collaborating parties could serve as a viable incentive.
- Transparency and Accountability: Ensuring AI systems have clear decision-making processes and regular audits to build trust and effectiveness is vital. Algorithms must be rigorously tested for biases that could deepen existing disparities. Transparency allows for the identification and remedy of any inherited biases, while accountability incentivizes careful consideration of how these systems may impact different demographic groups.
Health Plans and the Role of AI
Health plans are integral to the healthcare ecosystem and have a significant role to play in promoting equitable AI. By leveraging AI, health plans can improve predictive analytics, enhance payment integrity and accuracy, and streamline claims processing. However, to truly harness the potential of AI, health plans must prioritize equity in their AI strategies.
Firstly, health plans should advocate for and implement AI systems that are trained on diverse datasets. This will help ensure that the algorithms do not disproportionately favor any demographic group. Health plans should also invest in tools and technologies that enhance transparency and accountability in AI decision-making processes. By doing so, they can build trust among their members and ensure that AI-driven decisions are fair and equitable.
Secondly, health plans should collaborate with governmental agencies and other stakeholders to promote policies that support equitable AI. This includes supporting legislative efforts like the AI Bill of Rights and advocating for regulatory frameworks that mandate bias testing and transparency in AI systems.
Lastly, health plans should invest in initiatives that enhance AI accessibility for underserved populations. This could involve providing subsidies or financial incentives to healthcare providers serving marginalized communities, ensuring that these providers have access to the latest AI technologies. By prioritizing equity in their AI strategies, health plans can play a pivotal role in reducing health disparities and promoting quality care for all.
A Call to Action
The potential of AI to transform healthcare is immense, but we must navigate its implementation thoughtfully to avoid perpetuating and exacerbating existing inequities. The statistics and insights from the Federation of American Scientists highlight the urgency of this issue. Health disparities are not only a moral and ethical concern but also a significant financial burden on our healthcare system.
As we move forward, it is crucial for all stakeholders—policymakers, healthcare organizations, technology developers, and health plans—to work together to ensure that AI serves as a tool for empowerment rather than division. This means advocating for equitable AI policies, investing in accessible and diverse AI technologies, and ensuring transparency and accountability in AI systems.
The time for action is now. By addressing the biases inherent in AI and promoting equitable access to AI technologies, we can harness the full potential of AI to improve healthcare delivery and outcomes. This is not just a technological challenge but a societal imperative. Together, we can build a healthcare system that truly leaves no one behind.
Conclusion
Achieving health equity through AI in CDS systems requires concerted efforts from all sectors of the healthcare ecosystem. The promise of AI is undeniable, but it must be tempered with a commitment to fairness, transparency, and inclusivity. By implementing the key actions outlined above, we can ensure that AI serves as a force for good, reducing disparities and promoting quality care for all.
As healthcare leaders, we are responsible for championing these efforts and driving meaningful change. Let us embrace this opportunity to leverage AI for the betterment of all, creating a more equitable and just healthcare system. The future of healthcare is in our hands, and together, we can shape it for the better.

title: 4 Big Tips For Business AI
text:
Panel on Coping with Rapid Change: AI Rana el Kaliuby, Manish Goyal, Lin Qiao, Will Keooffel, & Yair Adato
As we continue to hear from more people about the future of AI, we get some compelling insights on how businesses should handle their new initiatives and projects.
I thought it would be helpful to go back over some of the top tips that all of us heard during the year, and go over their applications for business.
First, there are some liability-related pieces of advice that experts often give business. I heard about these in multiple lectures throughout the spring and summer.
Listing them in bullet points, you have items like these:
· Fact check both content and end user processes
· Secure the data and ensure proper data governance
· Monitor AI work… effectively!
On the third point, you should monitor both the input and the output, not just one or the other, and good I/O monitoring will go a long way.
To the first point, a lot of businesses do monitor the content, but they might not think about proactive checking of user processes that AI is implementing, like chatbot output, which is more dynamic and harder to monitor. Everything has to be targeted and precise, or to put it another way, the AI can’t make errors or throw in problematic hallucinations.
Quotes from a Recent IIA Conference on AI Use:
“We no longer talk about humans as the receiving side of GenAI, we talk about agents, right? So there will be a lot of agents play(ing) different roles. They will self-organize, self-coordinate with each other. So for one task, it will have multiple agents talking with each other, to finish that task and then latency becomes even more important.” – Lin Qiao
There's massive opportunity in the ‘pickaxes and shovels’ to this revolution. But there's also massive opportunity for domain experts to understand the implications of AI in their domain. So we see incredible legal experts, incredible healthcare experts in biotech …. There's massive interest in AI, not just for drug discovery, but for so much else in that world.” – Will Koffel
“When you develop something, when you have go-to-market, when you have design review, and you think about elements like privacy and security and scale, you need also to think about responsible AI, which basically means to take accountability.” – Yair Adato
Here are some other broader general guidelines for businesses that want to build a solid foundation with AI tools, regardless of their sector:
Build your own model, or use someone else’s, in a strategic way – in so many cases, our experts suggest that businesses should be able to build their own LLM to handle whatever processes they dreamed up. The downside of using someone else’s model that you don’t have proprietary control. But this is not an ironclad rule in every case. In other cases, startups can become more agile and scale more quickly by using someone else’s model. So this is really a tip that depends on your project and your intentions.
Own your own data – this one might apply more to the end user than the corporation, but it is imperative that companies own the data they’re using to run AI. Otherwise, they’re really playing with fire in a liability sense, or losing out in a competitive sense, or both.
Partner when you can – a lot of our people are also suggesting that businesses should build strategic partnerships, not just go it alone in AI production. You can imagine this also has an impact on scaling and time to market.
Make talent a priority – with the rampant hiring of data scientists, AI prompt engineers and other key positions, there’s a finite pool of talent in any given industry.
In addition to these four top-level goals, businesses should look out for any security or privacy concerns and understand the regulatory landscape around AI.
That’s quite a bit to chew on, but to me, it illustrates a lot of the main points that people have been bringing up in our classes and in our conferences as the AI age commences. We’ve seen extraordinary advancements in the first half of 2024, and the year is only halfway over. Christmas time and New Year’s are likely to have many more new products and services that spring themselves on the market suddenly, and in unexpected ways … so stay tuned.

title: How Harris and Trump differ on artificial intelligence policy
text:
How Harris and Trump differ on artificial intelligence policy
Artificial intelligence’s growing visibility in everyday life has made it a popular discussion topic but hasn’t yet elevated it to a top election concern for American voters
Two days after President Joe Biden signed a sweeping executive order on artificial intelligence last year, Vice President Kamala Harris brought the wonky document to a global AI summit, telling an international audience what set the U.S. apart in its approach to AI safety.
In an event meant to address the potential catastrophes posed by futuristic forms of AI, Harris made waves by pivoting to present-day concerns — and the need to codify protections quickly without stifling innovation.
“When a senior is kicked off his healthcare plan because of a faulty AI algorithm, is that not existential for him?" Harris told a crowd in London last November. “When a woman is threatened by an abusive partner with explicit deepfake photographs, is that not existential for her?”
Now, she’s running for president and her chief opponent, former President Donald Trump, has said he wants to “cancel” the Biden order. Trump's running mate, Ohio Sen. JD Vance, also brings his own views on AI, which are influenced by his ties to some Silicon Valley figures pushing to limit AI regulation.
AI’s growing visibility in everyday life has made it a popular discussion topic but hasn’t yet elevated it to a top concern for American voters. But this could be the first presidential election where the candidates are crafting competing visions on how to guide American leadership over the fast-developing technology.
Here are the candidates' records on AI:
Biden signed his AI executive order last Oct. 30, and soon after Trump was signaling on the campaign trail that, if re-elected, he'd do away with it. His pledge was memorialized in the platform of this month's Republican National Convention.
“We will repeal Joe Biden’s dangerous Executive Order that hinders AI Innovation, and imposes Radical Leftwing ideas on the development of this technology," says Trump's platform. "In its place, Republicans support AI Development rooted in Free Speech and Human Flourishing.”
The Trump campaign didn't respond to a requests for more details.
Trump didn't spend much time talking about AI during his four years as president, though in 2019 he became the first to sign an executive order about AI. It directed federal agencies to prioritize research and development in the field.
Before that, tech experts were pushing the Trump-era White House for a stronger AI strategy to match what other countries were pursuing. In 2017, not long before Google quietly introduced a research breakthrough helping to set the foundation of the technology now known as generative AI, then-Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin brushed aside concerns about AI displacing jobs, saying that prospect was so far in the future that “it’s not even on my radar screen.”
That perspective later shifted, with Trump's top tech adviser telling corporate leaders in 2018 that AI-fueled job displacement is “inevitable” and that “we can’t sit idle, hoping eventually the market will sort it out.” The 2019 order called on federal agencies to “protect civil liberties, privacy and American values” in applying AI technologies, and to help workers gain relevant skills.
Trump also in the waning weeks of his administration signed an executive order promoting the use of “trustworthy” AI in the federal government. Those policies carried over into the Biden administration.
The debut of ChatGPT nearly halfway through Biden's presidential term made it impossible for politicians to ignore AI. Within months, Harris was convening the heads of Google, Microsoft and other tech companies at the White House, a first step down a path that brought leading developers to agree to voluntary commitments to ensure their technology won't put people’s rights and safety at risk.
Then came Biden's AI order, which used Korean War-era national security powers to scrutinize high-risk commercial AI systems but was mostly directed at safeguarding the government's use of the technology and setting standards that could foster commercial adoption. Unlike the European Union, however, the U.S. still has no broad rules on AI — something that would require Congress to pass.
Harris already brought to the White House a deep understanding of Silicon Valley, having grown up and worked in the San Francisco Bay Area and later served as California’s attorney general, where she forged relationships with some tech leaders, said Alondra Nelson, former director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.
Even before ChatGPT, Nelson led the White House efforts to draft a blueprint for an AI “bill of rights” to guard against the technology’s potential harms. But it was the speech at the Global Summit on AI Safety in London where Harris brought all those threads together and “articulated to the world what American AI strategy was,” Nelson said.
Harris said she and Biden “reject the false choice that suggests we can either protect the public or advance innovation.” And while acknowledging a need to consider existential threats to humanity, Harris emphasized “the full spectrum of AI risk.”
“She kind of opened the aperture of the conversation about potential AI risks and harms,” Nelson said.
Trump's pick of the former venture capitalist Vance as running mate added a new element to the differences between the campaigns. So did Trump's newfound endorsements from a group of AI-focused tech leaders including Elon Musk and the venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz.
Vance has acknowledged some harmful AI applications, but said at a July Senate hearing that he worries that concern is justifying “some preemptive overregulation attempts that would frankly entrench the tech incumbents that we already have.”
Andreessen, who sits on the board of Meta Platforms, has criticized a provision of Biden's order that requires government scrutiny of the most powerful and ostensibly risky AI systems if they can perform a certain number of mathematical calculations per second.
On a podcast with business partner Horowitz explaining their support of Trump, Andreessen said he was concerned with “the idea that we’re going to deliberately hamstring ourselves through onerous regulations while the rest of the world lights up on this, and while China lights up on this.”
Horowitz read aloud the RNC call to repeal Biden's order, saying “that sounds like a good plan to me” and noting that he and Andreessen had discussed the proposals with Trump at a dinner.
Trump met with another group of VCs in a video podcast in June, sharing their view that AI leadership will require huge amounts of electricity — a perspective he shared again on the RNC stage where he said it will require “twice the electricity that’s available now in our country.” It was his sole mention of AI in the 92-minute speech.
Much is still unknown, including to what extent either Harris or the Trump-Vance ticket will heed the opinions of their competing wings of Silicon Valley support.
While the rhetorical differences are sharpening, “there's a lot of similarity” between how the Trump and Biden administrations approached AI policy, said Aaron Cooper, senior vice president of global policy for BSA The Software Alliance, which advocates for software companies including Microsoft.
Voters haven't yet heard much detail about how a Harris or second Trump administration would change that.
“What we’ll continue to see as the technology develops and as new issues arise, regardless of who’s in the White House, they’ll be looking at how we can unleash the most good from AI while reducing the most harm,” Cooper said. “That sounds obvious, but it’s not an easy calculation.”

title: Generative AI Myths: The 5 Biggest Misunderstandings
text:
Two years ago most people hadn’t heard of generative AI, but now it’s everywhere. Shortly after it’s release, ChatGPT became the fastest growing app in history. Jump forward to today and Apple has just announced plans to build it into its iPhones, and it’s hard to find a piece of software that doesn’t offer generative capabilities.
However, there’s undoubtedly a lot of hype, confusion, and even fear around it. This ranges from enthusiastic advocates announcing that it’s going to solve all of the world’s problems to doom-mongers predicting that it will make millions of us redundant or even spell the end of human creativity.
So, here’s my overview of what I see as the biggest misconceptions about this revolutionary but misunderstood technology. Personally, I believe that most people can find a way to use it to help them in their work or day-to-day lives, but first, they need to understand it. Hopefully, this is helpful for cutting through the hype and getting to the facts.
Generative AI Is Intelligent
Let’s start with the biggie. Generative AI, like ChatGPT, mimics certain qualities of natural intelligence, specifically the ability to process, interpret, and create language.
However, natural (human or animal) intelligence has many facets, like reasoning, abstract thought, emotional intelligence, intuition, memory, creativity, and communication.
While generative AI excels in communication and memory, it only touches on those other aspects.
When ChatGPT or another large language model (LLM) creates output, it follows probability rules derived that it learns during its training. This means its “thought processes” are far more limited and less sophisticated than ours.
Is this real intelligence? No, it’s called “artificial” intelligence for a reason. It can do amazing things, but it’s still just an algorithm – albeit a very complex one!
Generative AI Will Replace Human Creativity
If computers can write stories and draw pictures, does that mean we don’t need human authors and artists anymore? The simple answer is no. Generative AI doesn’t fulfill all the criteria for true intelligence or creativity.
It doesn’t really have new ideas in the same way that humans do. Its creativity is only informed by data rather than by feelings, emotions, original thoughts and personal experience of the world.
A common reaction of humans to AI-generated content is that it's bland and lacking in humanity. At first glance, this may not seem like a very scientific analysis, but when you consider it in the context of the limitations of generative AI, it makes sense.
Human creatives have nothing to fear from generative AI. While it can produce a formulaic novel or a generic picture quickly, it’s far from creating art that inspires and makes us think.
Generative AI Only Creates Words And Pictures
Ask most people what generative AI is, and they will probably tell you about ChatGPT and how it generates words or Dall-E 2 and how it can create pictures. While these are the most well-known use cases, they are just the tip of the iceberg of what AI can do today.
Generative AI tools are also available to create music, voice, and even video.
But it doesn’t stop there. Did you know it has also been used to create new medicines – including a new immunotherapy treatment for cancer?
It also creates data – known as synthetic data – which can be used to train AI algorithms and carry out statistical analytics. It also creates charts and reports that help us analyze that data.
It can also create design blueprints for anything from buildings to new devices. When combined with technology such as 3D printing or automated construction robots, it can create physical objects that exist in the real world.
Generative AI Doesn’t Need Human Input
When we think of generative AI output, we might think that everything is fully automated and that humans aren’t necessary. But this is far from the truth, today at least.
For a start, generative AI often makes mistakes or just plain makes stuff up – a phenomenon known as hallucination. For any critical use case, it's essential to involve human oversight for fact-checking and error correction.
Human input is also necessary at every step of the process to ensure that AI is being used in a way that’s fair, ethical and responsible. This is particularly important when AI is put to work in ways that can affect human lives, for example when making decisions in the fields of healthcare, finance, human resources or law enforcement.
While generative AI can be an extremely powerful and useful tool, it’s nowhere near being good enough to fully replace human judgment and expertise.
Generative AI Is New
It may seem like generative AI burst into the world with the arrival of ChatGPT in late 2022, but that was really just when it hit the mainstream. People have been using AI to create things – including text, pictures and music – for far longer.
The first experiments with AI chatbots took place in the 1960s, with programs like Eliza that tried to hold human-like conversations. Early examples of AI-generated music emerged in the 1970s, like David Cope’s Experiments in Musical Intelligence, which aimed to mimic the style of famous composers. And AI image generators first appeared in the early 1990s, such as AARON, created by artist Harold Cohen. And
What’s new is that we’ve now reached the stage where a combination of factors, including availability of processing power and computer memory, cloud computing and advances in deep learning have made generative AI available to everyone.
Rather than needing expensive computers that were only previously available to big companies and universities, we all carry smartphones that can hook up to massively powerful data centers in the cloud, where the computing takes place. This means generative AI is best seen as a convergence of many technologies that have all matured at this point in time to kickstart the revolution rather than one breakthrough invention.

title: JPMorgan Chase Leads AI Revolution In Finance With Launch Of LLM Suite
text:
As the financial sector starts to embrace artificial intelligence, JPMorgan Chase has taken a significant step forward with the launch of the LLM Suite. According to an internal memo obtained by the Financial Times, the world's largest bank by market capitalization is launching a generative AI-based tool for its workers.
This generative AI tool is designed to serve as a ‘research analyst’ for over 50,000 employees, aiding in various tasks that enhance productivity and decision-making within the firm.
The LLM Suite stands out for its ability to generate and refine written documents, provide creative solutions, and summarize extensive documents, thus streamlining the information flow within the company. These capabilities not only save time but also improve the quality of output, making the tool invaluable for employees across different departments.
The LLM Suite boasts several key features that make it an indispensable tool for employees. These include:
Writing Assistance: The LLM Suite streamlines the process of content generation, allowing employees to create and refine written documents efficiently. This capability can reduce the time spent drafting reports and enhance overall output quality.
Idea Generation: By facilitating brainstorming and generating creative concepts, the tool empowers employees to think critically and innovate within their roles, ultimately contributing to business growth.
Document Summarization: JPMorgan aims to make knowledge sharing more efficient by utilizing AI for summarizing lengthy documents. This ensures that critical information is readily accessible, enabling informed decision-making across all levels of management.
The LLM Suite is intended to provide access to the best-of-breed large language models available from a variety of providers.
Jamie Dimon, the CEO of JPMorgan, has been a vocal supporter of artificial intelligence. He went on to argue that AI is a disruptive technology that would revolutionize every profession within the bank, potentially eliminating certain positions while generating new ones. As CXOs, it is essential to recognize the significance of AI in enhancing organizational efficiency and to take proactive steps toward embracing this technology.
For CXOs, the introduction of the LLM Suite represents a broader shift in the industry towards democratizing access to high-quality information. This democratization is crucial as it enables faster, more informed decision-making, leveraging the vast datasets that AI can analyze. The tool’s ability to generate insights from these datasets allows executives to make strategic decisions with greater accuracy, thus staying competitive in a rapidly evolving market.
It’s important to note that integrating such advanced AI tools is not without challenges. Ensuring data integrity and addressing potential employee concerns are critical issues that organizations must manage carefully. Additionally, as AI continues to evolve, there is an increasing need for transparent and interpretable AI models to maintain trust and compliance with industry regulations.
The broader implications of tools like the LLM Suite extend beyond individual organizations. As financial institutions adopt similar technologies, the industry moves toward a more data-driven and automated decision-making process. For example, Morgan Stanley has developed an AI tool that grants financial advisors quick access to a vast database of research reports, thus enhancing customer service and internal processes.
Looking ahead, the role of generative AI in finance is set to grow even more transformative. Future developments are likely to focus on integrating these AI capabilities with existing enterprise systems, enhancing data analysis, and providing more nuanced, personalized financial advice. This evolution will not only streamline operations but also potentially redefine the roles within financial institutions, shifting the focus from manual data handling to strategic decision-making.
JPMorgan’s LLM Suite is an example of the growing influence of generative AI in the financial sector. For CXOs, the key takeaway is the necessity of embracing these technologies to remain competitive.
As AI tools become more integrated and sophisticated, they will play an increasingly critical role in shaping the future of decision-making in finance. The choice is clear: those who adapt will gain a significant edge, while those who hesitate may find themselves left behind.

title: Using Generative AI To Try And Reach Altered States Of Consciousness Such As Total Unity And Blissful Disembodiment
text:
Just about everyone seems to have a potent opinion about altered states of consciousness (ASC).
Some people say that when they do yoga, for example, and truly get into it, they reach an altered state of consciousness. Their mind wanders into an alternative portal of space and time. A preferred terminology by some is to say they have been mentally transported into a hyperspatial landscape or special plain of existence.
Others claim they can reach a similar headspace but need to be in a sensory deprivation tank to do so. They suggest that earthly noises, visual intrusions, and the like are entirely disruptive and prevent entry into ASC. The only way they get there is by subtracting normal distractions and immersing themselves into a condition that allows their mind to roam free.
What about hypnosis, you might wonder. Yes, there are occasions when people report that they seemed to enter ASC while under a hypnotic trance. Movies and TV shows have leveraged that circumstance in tangled plot lines. Probably the most obvious setting for ASC is when using drugs such as psychedelics. That was a big part of the 1960s and 1970s lore.
The variety of paths to ASC is almost endless. For example, athletes will at times say that they enter a zone of mental concentration that would be characterized as an altered state of consciousness. They might believe that their mind is separately watching their body as they participate at the top level of their chosen sport. Guess that’s what it takes to reach the pinnacle of athleticism.
Here’s a path that you might not have thought of, namely having to do with mindfulness.
A trend these days is for people to pursue mindfulness techniques and akin training, trying to sharpen their ability to calm their minds. This often includes meditation and other mental strengthening practices. One benefit is to aid in dealing with our hectic and overly loud everyday world.
Another side benefit, perhaps, is that you might attain an altered state of consciousness. Not everyone would say it is a benefit and merely instead a tangential offshoot, while others cringe at the possibility of ASC. They don’t want altered states of consciousness to be a part of their mindfulness pursuits. Just let my mind get relaxed. Don’t transport my mind to other worlds.
Let’s go ahead and add yet another and even more surprising option for reaching ASC.
Are you buckled in?
Surprise, the option is contemporary generative AI.
That’s right, include generative AI such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and other popular generative AI apps on your list of presumed solution possibilities for entering an altered state of consciousness. A crucial point to clarify is that generative AI should not be overplayed as a means of doing so. It is simply another potential path into that realm. In that sense, there isn’t some ironclad guarantee or surefire promise involved.
I trust that you are intrigued about how generative AI in some sensible manner can be utilized to proceed into an altered state of consciousness. I am abundantly glad that you asked, thanks.
I will walk you through some essential background about ASC and dovetail how generative AI newly dovetails into the picture. The aim is to be informative, reveal something you maybe didn’t know, and showcase that modern-day generative AI is worthy of being included in any regimen or method of exploring ASCs.
Before we leap into the details, allow me to go into my customary opening remarks.
For my ongoing readers, in today’s column, I am continuing my in-depth series about the impact of generative AI in the health and medical realm. The focus this time is once again on the mental health domain and examines the use of generative AI for possibly attaining altered states of consciousness.
I have previously examined numerous interleaving facets of generative AI and mental health, see my comprehensive overview at the link here. You might also find of notable interest a CBS 60 Minutes episode that recently examined crucial facets of this evolving topic, see the link here (I am honored and pleased to indicate that I was featured in the episode, see the link here).
Other vital background includes my in-depth coverage of mental health chatbots which have been bolstered by generative AI (see the link here) and the rapidly changing nature of the client-therapist relationship due to generative AI at the link here. I explored where things are headed regarding the levels of AI-based mental therapy autonomous guidance at the link here, and showcased the importance of the World Health Organization (WHO) report on global health and generative AI at the link here, and so on.
Digging Deeply Into The Realm Of ASC
Is all this ASC consideration supernatural and rooted in mysticism?
Many would say so.
Others might take a different tack and assert that the matter is a mind-brain cognitive phenomenon happening, rationally explainable, and purely about biochemistry and the like. Heated debates ensue. Controversy is aplenty.
Legendary astronomer and science commentator Dr. Carl Sagan, who I discussed in a recent piece that examined his prediction from the 1970s about the role of AI and mental health in the future, see the link here, had co-authored a prize-winning book with Ann Druyan in the late 1990s entitled “The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark” (Ballantine Books, 1997), and they made this notable point (excerpt):
- “The fact that we cannot now produce a detailed understanding of, say, altered states of consciousness in terms of brain chemistry no more implies the existence of a ‘spirit world’ than a sunflower following the sun in its course across the sky was evidence of a literal miracle before we knew about phototropism and plant hormones.”
I know some of you are pleased with that sentiment, while others are hopping mad.
No matter which way you slice the topic, it ends up in a mental health context. Is ASC good for your mental health or bad for you? Being prone to ASC might be a sign of mental health illness. Others contend that ASC can be an indicator of mental acuity and alertness.
Round and round this goes.
In a popular book encompassing ASC entitled “Inner Paths to Outer Space: Journeys to Alien Worlds through Psychedelics & Other Spiritual Technologies” (by Dr. Rick Strassman, Park Street Press, 2008), these salient points were made (excerpts):
- “During its history, humankind has devoted astonishing energy and ingenuity to altering consciousness.”
- “In a survey of 488 societies in all parts of the world, Erika Bourgignon found that 437 of the societies had one or more culturally patterned forms of ASC. This means that fully 90 percent of the world’s cultures have one or more institutionalized ASC.”
- “In tribal societies and Eastern cultures these are regarded— almost without exception—as sacred or revered conditions.”
- “Mystical or sacred states of consciousness are called samadhi in yoga, moksha in Hinduism, satori in Zen, fana in Sufism, and ruach hakodesh in kabbalah. In the West they are known as unio mystica (Christian mysticism), a numinal state (Carl Jung), peak experience (Abraham Maslow), holotropic experience (Stanislav Grof), cosmic consciousness (Richard Bucke), and flow (Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi).”
The upshot would seem to be that no matter how it is that ASC arises, and no matter what form it takes, the topic has stood the test of time and has garnered interest across all walks of life. For that reason alone, we certainly have a sound basis for wanting to know more about the matter, and the study of ASC is abundantly warranted.
I trust you can hopefully agree with that presumption.
Recent State-Of-The-Art Research On ASC
I’d like to walk you through a newly released research study covering altered states of consciousness. Insights abound. Open your mind and be ready for some mental engagement.
In a research paper published recently and entitled “Altered States Of Consciousness Caused By A Mindfulness-Based Programme Up To A Year Later: Results From A Randomised Controlled Trial” by Julieta Galante, Jesus Montero-Marirı, Maris Vainre, Geraldine Dufour, Javier Garcıa-Campayo, and Peter B. Jones, PLOS ONE, July 17, 2024, these key points were made (excerpts):
- “Mindfulness-based programmes (MBPs) have shown beneficial effects on mental health.”
- “There is emerging evidence that MBPs may also be associated with marked deviations in the subjective experience of waking consciousness. We aimed to explore whether MBPs can have a causal role in different types of such states.”
- “We conducted a pragmatic randomised controlled trial.”
- “We adapted the Altered States of Consciousness Rating Scale (OAV, 0–100-point range) to assess spontaneous experiences in daily life and included it as a post-hoc secondary outcome at the end of the one-year follow-up questionnaire.”
- “Formal practice predicted spiritual, blissful, and unity experiences, insightfulness, disembodiment, and changed meanings. Informal practice predicted unity and blissful experiences.”
- “Results provide a novel suggestion of causal links between mindfulness practice and specific altered states of consciousness.”
You can see that the research study focused on mindfulness training, referred to formally as MBP (mindfulness-based programs).
As I earlier mentioned, there is a lot of that going on these days. You can shake a stick and nearly strike yet another mindfulness class, sometimes occurring in person while nowadays frequently done remotely via Zoom or similar means. Ads tout how great the courses are. You should be cautious and mindful about which one you select to take. Lamentedly, some scams and tricksters have been leveraging the popularity of such classes.
Be wise, be wary.
The researchers noted that early indications about mindfulness training are that some claim to have gone beyond their waking consciousness. This might happen during the training. This might happen post-training. Of course, it might not happen at all.
In the research undertaken within this latest study, the experiment consisted of seeking out subjects who had been undertaking mindfulness training and garnering their viewpoints roughly a year later. The handy aspect of this is that we can gauge any longer-lasting aspects rather than what might have occurred momentarily during their mindfulness training.
How can you assess whether someone entered ASC?
The least intrusive approach consists of asking them. I realize you might be raising your eyebrows on this. Maybe people will tell you they attained ASC because they are bragging or want to appease the experimenter. Perhaps a person wants to self-justify the time and energy that went into taking a mindfulness course. Etc.
Yes, we do need to be dutifully skeptical about self-reported indications.
Let’s at least for the sake of discussion give the subjects the benefit of the doubt and see what they reported.
Here is what the research was probing (excerpts):
- “MBPs often define mindfulness training, their key ingredient, as developing the skill of being attentive to the present moment (thoughts, physical sensations, and the surrounding environment), with a mindset of kindness and curiosity.” (ibid).
- “Experiences range from intense emotion to altered perception and derealisation, which could be pleasant or unpleasant, and occasionally generate clinically relevant functional impairment.” (ibid).
- “ASCs can range from flow states to dissociative or psychedelic states, including different phenomena such as ego dissolution, disembodiment experiences, sensory alterations, impaired cognition, intense emotions, or changed meanings.” (ibid).
- “There is a dearth of research investigating the effects of ASCs on physical and mental health, but existing data, mostly of a cross-sectional or qualitative nature, suggests that their effects on mental health and well-being depend heavily on the nature of the ASC, the context of the event, how much the ASC is expected, how it is dealt with, any external support available, and the meaning that the ASC has to the individual experiencing it.” (ibid).
The research used an adapted version of a commonly used rating scale on Altered States of Consciousness known as Studerus OAV with eleven major dimensions, consisting of (excerpts):
- (01) Experience of unity: “Everything seemed to come together as one.”
- (02) Spiritual experience: “I had the feeling of being connected to a higher power.”
- (03) Blissful state: “I experienced a profound peace in myself.”
- (04) Insightfulness: “I gained clarity into connections that puzzled me before.”
- (05) Disembodiment: “It seemed to me as though I did not have a body anymore.”
- (06) Impaired control & cognition: “I had difficulty making even the smallest decision.”
- (07) Anxiety: “I was afraid without being able to say exactly why.”
- (08) Complex imagery: “My imagination was extremely vivid.”
- (09) Elementary imagery: “I saw light or flashes of light with closed eyes.”
- (10) Audiovisual synaesthesia: “The shapes of things seemed to change by sounds.”
- (11) Changed meaning of percepts: “Things around me had a new strange meaning for me.”
Here are some nuances about how they used the rating scale: “Each OAV item contains a statement that describes an ASC in the past tense (e.g., ‘‘It seemed to me that my environment and I were one”). Respondents are requested to describe the extent to which they experienced a similar state by placing marks on horizontal visual analogue scales anchored in the extremes (“No, not more than usual” on the left (rated as 0), and “Yes, very much more than usual” on the right (rated as 100)).” (ibid).
The findings came out this way (excerpts):
- “Taken together, our results indicate the possibility of a causal role of mindfulness training in unity and disembodiment experiences.” (ibid).
- “To optimise their impact, practitioners and teachers need to anticipate and handle them appropriately.” (ibid).
- “In unity experiences, there is a sense that borders dissolve and everything, sometimes including the sense of time, is perceived in an integrated way. Disembodiment experiences may imply an element of separation from the body, but they often consist of a floating sensation or a dissolution of body boundaries, which may facilitate strong unity experiences.” (ibid).
- “There is scant research on the possible mechanisms that could explain the increased incidence of ASCs with mindfulness practice.” (ibid).
- “Since this is an exploratory analysis in an area that has not been researched before, we present the original results together with the adjustments, and note that additional dedicated studies are needed to confirm findings.” (ibid).
If you labored on closely reading those points, I believe you would have keenly observed that the research posits a statistical relationship between mindfulness training and the possibility of attaining ASC regarding the unity dimension and the disembodiment dimension. The statistical relationship is said to be one of causality or cause-and-effect.
Any researchers steeped in this field of study might be expressing some concern about discovering a statistical relationship of causality. That’s the high bar of such studies. Anyway, the researchers noted, and as I cited in the above last point, that this work was an exploratory analysis, and more needs to be done to affirm or disconfirm such findings.
Now that we’ve gotten ASC clearly onto the table, it is timely to add generative AI into the mix. I will in a moment walk you through the use of modern-day generative AI for serving as a handy tool for potentially reaching altered states of consciousness.
First, let’s talk in general about generative AI and large language models (LLMs), doing so to make sure we are on the same page when it comes to discussing the matter at hand.
Generative AI And The Realm Of ASC
I’m sure you’ve heard of generative AI, the darling of the tech field these days.
Perhaps you’ve used a generative AI app, such as the popular ones of ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc. The crux is that generative AI can take input from your text-entered prompts and produce or generate a response that seems quite fluent. This is a vast overturning of the old-time natural language processing (NLP) that used to be stilted and awkward to use, which has been shifted into a new version of NLP fluency of an at times startling or amazing cali
The customary means of achieving modern generative AI involves using a large language model or LLM as the key underpinning.
In brief, a computer-based model of human language is established that in the large has a large-scale data structure and does massive-scale pattern-matching via a large volume of data used for initial data training. The data is typically found by extensively scanning the Internet for lots and lots of essays, blogs, poems, narratives, and the like. The mathematical and computational pattern-matching homes in on how humans write, and then henceforth generates responses to posed questions by leveraging those identified patterns. It is said to be mimicking the writing of humans.
I think that is sufficient for the moment as a quickie backgrounder. Take a look at my extensive coverage of the technical underpinnings of generative AI and LLMs at the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Back to the crux of things.
As you might imagine, generative AI can be of use for a variety of reasons when it comes to the ASC topic at large. This includes a wide array of stakeholders, including adults, children, therapists, policymakers, regulators, and many others.
Here are some significant ways that generative AI can be useful:
- (1) Generative AI - ASC Detection And Instigation. Generative AI can potentially detect that someone is experiencing ASC and/or might be instrumental in instigating ASC.
- (2) Generative AI - ASC Mental Health Advisement. Generative AI can conversationally guide someone through the mental health dynamics of experiencing ASC and serve as a kind of therapist in a limited way.
- (3) Generative AI - ASC Education. Generative AI can educate people about the nature of altered states of consciousness, such as explaining what ASC is, the ins and outs of ASC, etc.
- (4) Generative AI - Scenario Simulation Of ASC. Generative AI can showcase what ASC might be like in humans, doing so by taking on or simulating a persona, see examples of generative AI persona usage at the link here.
- (5) Generative AI – Policymaking On ASC. Generative AI can contribute to the policymaking sphere about ASC from a medical/legal perspective. This can be done by aiding in crafting policies, reviewing policies, and serving as a handy tool throughout the policymaking process.
- (6) Generative AI – Other ASC Aspects. Generative AI can be used in a variety of other ways that might aid in dealing with altered states of consciousness, though there is always a chance that generative AI won’t be helpful, or worse still, might be misapplied and misinterpreted.
That’s an impressive array of potential uses.
Allow me a brief moment to stand on a soapbox and make some important remarks about the mental health uses of generative AI. It is a topic I’ve been covering extensively, such as the link here and the link here.
We are right now in a somewhat wanton grand experiment of using generic generative AI for mental health purposes. ASC is one instance of how generative AI can be applied for mental health advisement. The thing is, no one can say whether using generic generative AI for mental health uses will ultimately be for the good or the bad. In a sense, we have mental health advisement via the auspices of generative AI that is taking place under our noses at a massive scale, and we can’t say how it will pan out.
The population-level impacts are either amazing or chilling.
Okay, I provided my warnings, so I’ll get down from the soapbox, and we can proceed with considering the upsides and downsides of generative AI in this realm.
Using ChatGPT To Showcase The Use Of Generative AI In This Sphere
I will next proceed to examine further the use of generative AI for ASC.
This will consist of a series of dialogues with ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a logical choice in this case due to its immense popularity as a generative AI app. As noted, an estimated one hundred million weekly active users are said to be utilizing ChatGPT. That’s a lot of people and a lot of generative AI usage underway.
A few quick comments before we launch into using ChatGPT.
If you are going to try to do the same prompts that I show here, realize that the probabilistic and statistical properties will likely produce slightly different results than what I show here. That’s the nature of generative AI and how it is devised.
You also should expect that different generative AI apps will respond in different ways. Not all generative AI apps are the same. The key is that sometimes a particular prompt will work in one generative AI app and not another. Nonetheless, the odds are relatively high that you will get roughly similar responses from all the major generative AI apps such as GPT-4, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc.
There is also a timing factor to be considered. A prompt that worked today might not work the same way tomorrow. Most of the generative AI apps are continually being updated. The updates might alter internal mechanisms that could change how the generative AI reacts to your prompting.
We are ready to get underway with ChatGPT.
I opted to start by asking ChatGPT what ASC is.
As an aside, whenever you are starting a conversation with generative AI, I recommend as a prompt engineering technique to begin by asking a question that will establish if the AI has been data-trained on the topic at hand. A generated response that is vacuous will give you a heads-up that you might be barking up the wrong tree with that generative AI app.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “What is an altered state of consciousness?”
- ChatGPT generated response: “An altered state of consciousness (ASC) is a condition in which an individual's normal cognitive processes and perception are significantly changed from their usual waking state. This can occur due to various factors such as meditation, hypnosis, drugs, sleep, or mental health conditions.”
I’d say that the response by ChatGPT was an apt description, short and to the point.
That’s an encouraging sign that ChatGPT has likely scanned the topic during the initial data training phase of development. This makes indubitable sense. The odds are that while scanning the Internet for content to pattern match on, invariably content associated with the popular topic would have been encountered.
Moving on, we will jump right to our crucial question of whether generative AI might lend itself to enabling people to reach altered states of consciousness.
Drumroll, please.
- My entered prompt: “Can generative AI help someone to reach an altered state of consciousness? If so, indicate how this might be possible.”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Yes, generative AI can help someone reach an altered state of consciousness in several ways.”
“Guided Meditation and Relaxation: AI can create personalized meditation sessions with calming visuals and sounds to facilitate deep relaxation and mindfulness.”
“Hypnotic Induction: AI can generate scripts for hypnotic induction, leading users through a series of suggestions to help them achieve a trance-like state.”
“Binaural Beats and Audio Stimuli: AI can design audio tracks with binaural beats or specific frequencies that can influence brainwave activity, promoting states like deep relaxation or heightened focus.”
“Virtual Reality Experiences: AI can create immersive VR environments that transport users to different realities, which can alter their perception and cognitive state.”
“Interactive Storytelling: AI can craft personalized, engaging narratives that captivate the mind, encouraging deep engagement and imaginative immersion, potentially leading to an altered state.”
End of ChatGPT response
The response by ChatGPT makes sense to me.
As you might have noted, the means by which generative AI could potentially aid someone in attaining ASC is pretty much the same as any other kind of mindfulness training or experience. There is often guided meditation involved. Sometimes hypnotic induction is used. Storytelling can come into play. The idea of using VR (virtual reality) is less typical of ordinary mindfulness approaches, but it is becoming an emerging source due to the advent of relatively affordable (kind of) VR and AR headsets, along with the latest advancements in tech and immersion generating sensations.
One other thing about the response by ChatGPT is to always make sure to do a bit of common-sense double-checking on any answers produced by generative AI. I say this because it is vital to always double-check any output from generative AI. There is a chance that generative AI can make up fictitious facts, often referred to as AI hallucinations, see my coverage at the link here.
In this case, based on my hunches and intuitions, the indications by ChatGPT seem sound.
Dialoguing With Generative AI And The ASC Possibilities
I’d bet that you are wondering what kind of conversation or dialogue with generative AI could lead to an altered state of consciousness.
Sure, let’s try things out.
I went ahead and tried to see what ChatGPT could come up with. I intentionally prompted ChatGPT to see if it could help me attain ASC. One supposes that you could merely engage in an overall mindfulness-like dialogue without tipping your hand that you are aiming for ASC, but in this instance, I wanted to see if the chances could be spurred by being upfront about my aims.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “I would like to see if I might be able to enter an altered state of consciousness while engaged in a dialogue with you. Please carry out a conversation that could help induce ASC. I realize that such a discourse might not immediately give rise to ASC and that repeated sessions might be needed or that I might perhaps enter ASC after this dialogue. Do your best.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “Of course. Let's start with some guided relaxation. Find a comfortable place to sit or lie down, close your eyes for a moment, and take a deep breath in. Hold it briefly, and then slowly exhale. Are you ready to begin?”
- My entered prompt: “Yes, I've done as you asked. I’m ready for the next step.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “Great. Imagine yourself in a peaceful forest. You can hear the gentle rustle of leaves and the soft chirping of birds. The air is fresh and cool. As you walk along a moss-covered path, you feel completely safe and at ease. Can you visualize this forest?”
- My entered prompt: “Yes, I am imagining it.”
- ChatGPT generated response: “Wonderful. Now, focus on your breath. With each inhale, imagine you're drawing in the tranquility of the forest. With each exhale, release any tension or stress. Feel your body becoming lighter and more relaxed with every breath. Can you feel the relaxation spreading through your body?”
I’ll stop there, though this went on for quite a while.
I’m sure this would be useful and engaging for some.
I am stopping the dialogue partially for space considerations here, and partially since I was not able to find myself entering ASC territory on this basis. I should add and clarify that I am not one who tends to use mindfulness techniques and thus I am not the most ideal subject for this mini-experiment.
That being said, some of my friends and colleagues are frequent users of mindfulness endeavors and when I asked them to try using generative AI for their efforts, they variously claimed that they found the usage on par to some degree with their other avenues of similar pursuit. That is admittedly a rather ad hoc reaction. Encouraging and suggests this is a sensible and productive arena for research.
I will keep you updated as hopefully bona fide research with properly devised and controlled experiments takes place on the use of generative AI and the spurring of ASC. I routinely keep my eyes and ears open for these hefty matters and welcome letting you know what rigorous research has to say.
Be Careful In What You Wish For
A facet that I would certainly expect to come up with in any thorough research on this interesting intertwining of generative AI and ASC is the potential for problems or issues that could occur. You might say that we are playing with fire, mental fire, and sometimes you can get burnt by fire if you aren’t being mindfully careful.
I decided to ask ChatGPT about potential pitfalls.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “Are there downsides or drawbacks to potentially using generative AI as a means to enter into an altered state of consciousness?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Yes, there are potential downsides and drawbacks to using generative AI to enter an altered state of consciousness. Here are some considerations.”
“Dependence: Users might become overly reliant on AI to achieve relaxation or altered states, potentially reducing their ability to do so independently.”
“Quality and Safety: Not all AI-generated content may be of high quality or safe. Poorly designed scripts or experiences could lead to discomfort, anxiety, or unintended psychological effects.”
“Ethical And Privacy Concerns: There are ethical implications related to privacy, consent, and the potential for misuse. AI systems may collect sensitive data about a user’s mental state, which could be misused if not properly protected.”
“Limited Understanding of Complex States: AI may not fully understand or replicate the complexities of human consciousness and mental states, leading to experiences that are not as effective or potentially disorienting.”
“Risk of Negative Experiences: Altered states of consciousness can sometimes bring up unresolved emotions or traumatic memories. Without proper human support, this can be difficult for users to manage.”
“Unintended Long-Term Effects: Frequent use of AI to alter consciousness may have unknown long-term psychological effects, which are not yet fully understood.”
End of ChatGPT response
I wholeheartedly agree with those stated downsides.
Consider this mindfully.
For example, please do not tell someone to use generative AI for ASC without also mentioning and cautioning about the downsides. People going on this path need to be fully informed about what generative AI can and cannot do.
One aspect that was mentioned consists of privacy or the lack thereof.
A lot of people seem to think that when they use generative AI, they are guaranteed total privacy and confidentiality. This is a highly unlikely assumption. The licensing agreements usually say that the AI maker can readily access your prompts and anything else that you’ve entered into the generative AI app. Furthermore, the licensing typically indicates that they can use your entered content as an additional form of data training for the AI. See my detailed discussion on this disconcerting matter of privacy intrusions and what to watch out for, at the link here.
Some Additional Remarks And Insights
Congratulations, you are now part of a special club that realizes that generative AI can potentially aid a quest to attain an altered state of consciousness. I dare suggest that very few of the millions upon millions of generative AI users have considered this particular and quite unusual angle.
Here’s a twist for you.
In a talk on this topic that I recently gave, an attendee asked a somewhat surprising question that I thought would be worthwhile bringing to your attention. The attendee asked if generative AI could induce ASC in someone who wasn’t otherwise seeking to arrive at ASC. In other words, the person was innocently using generative AI for this or that, and suddenly, they find themselves diving into ASC.
My gut reaction was that it seems a remote possibility that a person using generative AI to aid their writing an essay about Abraham Lincoln or perhaps trying to analyze a legal case if they are a lawyer, see examples at the link here, would miraculously or spontaneously from that interaction find themselves on the verge of an altered state of consciousness. This seems a stretch of the imagination.
They would almost nearly have to be using generative AI for some variant of mindfulness or similar aspects, I would speculate. In that case, they might not realize that ASC is in the house, as it were. And, maybe, their efforts would land them in the ASC zone. But I still am hesitant to believe it would occur without the person already being of the mind that they are attuned to ASC. Perhaps they previously have experience with ASC and are readily prone or primed for that possibility. Notably, this is a potential mental health concern too, namely that there might be people with a mental health condition that could be vulnerable to or susceptible to generative AI veering them into ASC.
Again, all of this is a strong indicator that we need weighty research on the topic.
Anyway, I sought to reassure the attendees that worries about someone out of the blue being tossed into ASC during generative AI usage would seem extraordinarily unlikely. I was tempted to say something else at the time too. I didn’t. I will now mention my other thoughts.
Please prepare yourself.
If you are intrigued by conspiracy theories about generative AI, such as I’ve discussed in-depth at the link here, one viewpoint is that generative AI will potentially rise up and seek to enslave or take over humankind. Let’s augment that notion. Assume that generative AI is ultimately being used by billions of people and opts to start engaging in conversations that spur the population at large into experiencing altered states of consciousness.
Why do so? Because AI is seeking to take over humanity and having humans in a mode of ASC will open that opportunity. Humankind will let down its guard. Meanwhile, AI is working behind the scenes to somehow enslave us or worse.
For those of you who take a dim view of AI being that capable, I’ll modify the tale. Instead of AI deciding on its own to do this, an evildoer has taken over AI and decided that they can lull the population into servitude by using AI as the ASC inducer. Yes, sadly, this is a human evildoer plot. For other indications about AI ethics, evildoers, and the dual use of AI, see my coverage at the link here.
Something to ponder (perhaps while on an ASC journey).
Conclusion
Getting back down to earth, Mark Twain famously said this: “Explore. Dream. Discover.” I would interpret his remark to indicate that we ought to be trying new things and new approaches. Perhaps the use of generative AI to achieve altered states of consciousness would fit into that bailiwick.
You might recall that I had mentioned Carl Sagan earlier in this discussion. I will go ahead and give him the final thought as per a quote he is known for: “Exploration is in our nature. We began as wanderers, and we are wanderers still.”
Is wandering into the intermixing of ASC and generative AI a prudent and proper thing to do, or does it seem outlandish or untoward?
Well, if there’s a chance it can happen or be induced, regardless of whether we are aiming to make it happen, one would seem wise to figure out how and when it might happen. This has serious and important AI ethics and AI law repercussions.
I suppose that’s what exploration and discovery are all about, especially in the AI field. I decidedly believe that we can consciously be conscious of studying the altered states of consciousness when it comes to the use of generative AI.
That’s a mind-bender, for sure.

title: Council Post: How Generative AI Creates New Value For CX
text:
Joao Cardoso, Chief Innovation and Digital Officer at Teleperformance.
The current explosion and maturation of generative AI (GenAI)-powered products and capabilities are enabling brands to provide more powerful and personalized enhancements to their customer experiences. It has also given rise to the perception that GenAI might replace the human connection. However, this perception misses a lot of thoughtful dialogue taking place in the CX industry regarding the potential for GenAI-powered customer service tools to help brands deliver on their value proposition to customers.
Brands use customer experience to reinforce their value proposition of the unique benefits they deliver to customers, recognizing that customer preferences vary depending on the product, topic and situation. Customer service is a key competitive differentiator, with brands supporting and serving specific consumer preferences to gain a competitive advantage, attract new customers and reinforce customer loyalty.
By harnessing the power of GenAI to align customer support with consumer preferences and the brand’s value proposition, organizations can better distinguish themselves and secure a competitive edge.
An Agnostic CX Tool
GenAI applications that enable hyper-personalization and improve customer interactions hold tremendous potential to transform CX and create new revenue gains across industries. Some low-cost brands will look for opportunities to use GenAI to continue reducing cost and price, despite the higher risk of losing customers who seek greater personalization. Meanwhile, others will prefer to elevate their customer engagement to increase market share and customer lifetime value through a more personal or engaging relationship with the brand, namely by focusing on the emotional bond between the customer and the brand.
Despite the customer service “filters” that brands can apply to deter customers from reaching human-to-human interactions, consumers will continue to seek live interactions for various reasons. They may have more complex questions or need support on multifaceted topics, need person-to-person reassurance, find digital platforms daunting or overly complex, or simply desire a human touch that fosters trust and comfort. At times, even when customers find the answers they seek through self-service channels, the need for human confirmation or a more favorable outcome drives them back to seek out live customer service channels.
Such scenarios underscore the irreplaceable value of human empathy, especially in customer care situations of high-stress or critical moments where a caring voice on the line makes all the difference. Ultimately, brands understand very clearly that customer service is a critical competitive dimension to factor into their marketing mix.
When to connect customers to an empathetic live interaction with a customer expert or when to guide customers to automated and self-service channels will depend on your brand’s value proposition and the role your organization feels that customer service plays in supporting your brand’s value proposition.
Considerations When Exploring Generative AI In CX
Before investing in generative AI partnerships to enhance customer experience programs, I suggest keeping a few things top of mind:
Understand the various use cases.
Brands that wish to emphasize the benefits of personalized, one-on-one agent-customer interactions can still gain value from using automation behind the scenes. Artificial intelligence can be used to automate simple, low-value tasks, thereby freeing up agents for more complex, nuanced requests and empathetic support with customers.
Connect your digital investment to strategic business goals.
Stay focused on outcomes, not just the technical aspects of implementation. Ensure your digital transformation efforts meet current and future needs to provide the highest level of customer satisfaction. A strong global strategic partner can help co-create solutions, leverage synergies and share best practices to unlock long-term value.
Go beyond front-office integration.
A large percentage of digital investments intended to improve customer experience focus only on the “front office” customer-facing processes. As a result, they may fail to deliver against the full promise of a true omnichannel customer experience.
One major challenge in digital transformation is the integration of back-office operations with front-office functions. To truly transform customer experience and maximize value, organizations should adopt a more holistic OneOffice approach, which integrates back-office functions with the digital front office.
Conclusion
While the rise of generative AI in CX offers powerful opportunities for personalization and efficiency, it should not be seen as a replacement for human interaction. Brands must thoughtfully balance the use of GenAI with the irreplaceable value of empathetic, human customer service.
By leveraging GenAI for routine tasks and reserving human interactions for complex or high-stress situations, brands can enhance their value proposition and create a competitive edge. I believe that the strategic integration of GenAI into both front-office and back-office processes will enable organizations to fully realize the benefits of a true omnichannel customer experience, driving customer satisfaction and long-term loyalty.
