Coefficient automates importing live data from platforms like Hubspot or Salesforce into Excel or Goole Sheets and can interface with ChatGPT to query your data in natural language.
Domo uses natural language conversations to guide you through the process of deploying analytics and extracting insights.
The plugin provides custom connectivity with Excel for ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Pro.
Talk directly to your data to get expert insights and analysis alongside customized reports.
Generative AI assistant provides quick answers and insights into business data.
It specializes in the in-depth analysis of text information, such as customer feedback reports.
Answer your important business questions with instant insights using Polymer’s PolyAI chatbot.
Conversational data discovery and dashboard building with built-in security features, works with any LLM.
Generative AI analytics designed to provide marketing insights.
AI-driven analytics platform that combines search and AI to enable natural language queries and automated insights generation.
Emphasizes data-driven storytelling and a collaborative approach to machine learning-powered analytics.

title: GitHub Launches Integrated Model Playground For AI Developers
text:
GitHub announced that it will make generative AI models more accessible to developers by tightly integrating with existing tools and features. This new capability, known as GitHub Models, allows developers to explore various models within the GitHub web interface. They can also test and compare different models without leaving their current environment.
GitHub Models provides a robust playground for developers to interact with leading models like Meta's Llama 3.1, OpenAI's GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, Cohere's Command, and Mistral AI's Mistral Large 2. This integration is especially useful for developers, who can now experiment with different models and configurations directly within GitHub Codespaces or Visual Studio Code, speeding up the process of developing AI applications from prototype to production.
The feature closely resembles the capabilities of model playgrounds offered by model providers and cloud providers, including Microsoft Azure. OpenAI was one of the first to launch a playground where users could test different parameters and even generate code based on the configuration. GitHub is now enabling similar features by integrating its command line tools, Codespaces, and Visual Studio Code.
While Azure provides a mature development environment and model playground, it is only available to subscribers and customers. Before accessing the model playground, a developer must first complete a pre-defined workflow specific to Azure. GitHub Models effectively bypasses this step, making the models immediately available to developers.
Because Azure is an enterprise platform, Microsoft must establish a rigorous process to ensure compliance and safety in accordance with responsible AI principles. This may cause delays in the availability of certain Azure models. Because GitHub caters to developers, the models can be made available immediately. Once the developers have evaluated and finalized a model on GitHub, they can switch to Azure and use the same mode, code, and configuration in production. This provides an on-ramp into Azure AI via GitHub.
The introduction of GitHub Models also positions GitHub as a viable alternative to platforms such as Hugging Face, which, while well-known for hosting model weights, lacks the deep integration with development tools that GitHub provides. By bridging this gap, GitHub allows developers to experiment with AI models while also quickly exporting and integrating their code into existing workflows.
This initiative is consistent with Microsoft's broader strategy to improve AI accessibility and usability. GitHub Models allows developers to leverage the power of generative AI on GitHub before seamlessly transitioning to Azure to scale their solutions. This integration furthers Microsoft's goal of providing a comprehensive, developer-friendly path from experimentation to deployment.
One important use case of GitHub Models is to allow educators and students to quickly experiment with generative AI models. GitHub has already announced that Professor David J. Malan will test GitHub Models in Harvard's CS50 this fall, making it easier for students to experiment with AI.
GitHub Models, like most of GitHub's new features, is available in a limited public beta, and developers must sign up to be added to the waitlist.
Microsoft is pulling out all the stops to accelerate the adoption of Azure AI. The introduction of GitHub Models marks a significant step in this direction.

title: Why Alibaba Is Key To China’s Global GenAI Leadership
text:
China has filed five times more GenAI patents than the U.S. in the last decade. That is more than 38,000 patent applications in GenAI, according to the World Intellectual Property Organization. China excels in finding applications of new technologies, and this is also the case in GenAI.
Applications ranging from autonomous driving – fueled by the electric vehicle boom led by Chinese carmakers BYD, NIO, Xpeng and others – to AI chatbots in ecommerce –by companies such as Alibaba and Bytedance. But perhaps it is the hidden champions such as NetEase that we should look out for. GenAI in China is transforming retailers and consumer journeys across sectors, and global executives are competing in the dark. Alibaba's experience is telling, and paves the way for China's GenAI transformation.
There are four actions that global business leaders can take from the lessons of the first applications of GenAI in China:
· Leverage China as an Innovation Hub for GenAI: Utilize China's rapid decision-making environment and flexible customer base as a testbed for new products and initiatives that are powered by GenAI.
· Caste a wide net: the GenAI race has just started, and business leaders would be wise to look at both the current leaders, from Microsoft to Alibaba, but also at the oceans of new players coming into the GenAI space.
· Leverage business value from GenAI: Chinese companies show the road to application of GenAI at scale. Either look and learn, or, even better, partner up to get access to the latest applications and business models.
· Protect your core: China’s GenAI is going to take the world in waves, better be prepared, from a data privacy and cybersecurity perspective, and with an eye on your competitive position.
All things considered, GenAI evolution at Alibaba is driven by an enterprise-wide transformation, a decade in the making.
Alibaba Is Getting Ready For GenAI At Scale
The recent past has been a roller-coaster ride at Alibaba. Alibaba went from untouchable in the 2010s to being challenged by competition, consumers and regulators alike in the 2020s. The time of fast growth is long gone, and Alibaba has been in search of mature management models and growth approaches while rethinking some of their diversifications. Alibaba’s challenges have come thick and fast, and they continue.
Then, in March 2023, the company announced one of the most drastic reorganization plans in its 24-year history, initially aimed at splitting into one holding group, six business groups, and numerous business companies, with IPO and financing plans quickly unfolding.
Notably, the divestiture of Alibaba Cloud and the planned IPO of Hema, its supermarket unit, were key moves in this restructuring, but within six months, these plans saw a dramatic shift. The divestiture of the cloud business was scrapped and Hema's IPO was paused, largely due to reduced investor interest and external policy changes.
Then, in October, an update by the USA on export control rules for advanced computing chips, aimed at restricting chip exports to China, directly affected Alibaba Cloud's ability to offer high-end computing services, leading to a halt in the cloud business split.
Concurrently, Alibaba underwent major executive changes. Zhang Yong stepped down as chairman and CEO and was replaced by Wu Yongming, who outlined a refined strategy focusing on technology-driven internet platform business, AI-driven technology business, and a global commercial network.
GenAI At Alibaba: Not The Next OpenAI
Alibaba is strengthening its core ecommerce business, while reevaluating their offline retail investments. At the same time, Alibaba maintains their investments in new technologies. This is apparent in their work on GenAI – although suffering from the U.S. government’s chip sanctions - as the leading contender from China.
Then Alibaba Cloud reinforced its AI ecosystem in November 2023 by open-sourcing a 72-billion-parameter general-purpose model. This move, aimed at becoming a computing power provider like Microsoft rather than a model developer like OpenAI, signals Alibaba Cloud's ambition to be a key player in the AI domain.
The country's large-model industry is still playing catch-up with GPT 3.5, but focuses on creating more applications based on large models compared to the West. This disparity is partly due to China’s comparative disadvantage in terms of access to quality data and high performing chip sets, but also a strategic choice that echoes many of China’s innovators’ long term preference for business application. The latter is something the central government wants to change, with a renewed focus on developing foundational technologies in China. It will just take time to take effect.
Masters Of GenAI Application
As Alibaba Cloud repositions itself in the AI wave, it faces the challenge of proving its mettle in technology and profitability. This shift reflects not just Alibaba's ambitions but also the changing landscape of China's tech industry, where innovation and strategic flexibility are crucial for sustained success.
The U.S. is likely to take the lead in making the most cutting-edge AI systems. Moreover, most U.S. companies have access to better training data. But, China has one superpower: building and commercializing applications at great speed. For decades China has been upgrading innovation from production processes to business models, eventually into fundamental technologies and organizational models. If anything, Chinese companies and entrepreneurs have been masters of application by recombining new and existing technologies and business models.
One example is the livestreaming industry in China. By a distance, the most developed in the world. Livestreaming uses a combination of existing video software technologies, computer vision and natural language process machine learning algorithms combined with an innovative business model that links ecommerce to entertainment. Case in point is the success of Alibaba's Taobao Live and global success of TikTok. New to the world? maybe not, but certainly with great innovation and impact.
GenAI Underdog NetEase Driving Real World Business Applications
Alibaba’s less well-known peer NetEase, has followed a different path from their mega competitors. NetEase has primarily focused on building virtual environments in gaming, digital communities and communication. Away from the limelight, and despite intense competition from Tencent, Alibaba, and JD.com, NetEase has managed to maintain a strong position.
The company navigates regulatory challenges and adapts to changes in policies related to market access and licensing requirements, especially in sectors like online education.
Moreover, it is reported to invest 15% in R&D (calculated from their financial results, https://ir.netease.com/) on an annual basis, part of which goes into a range of AI applications for virtual environments. NetEase has committed a substantial annual investment of at least US$1.4 billion for the development of large language models and other technological fields.
For instance, in a major move towards applying its AI and gaming technology to practical real-world applications, NetEase's AI arm, Fuxi Lab, has partnered with China State Construction Engineering Corp to develop smart robots for the construction industry.
China's GenAI advantage Still In The Making
It should come as no surprise that China is prioritizing the use and adoption of GenAI solutions. China has been in a state of economic reform for decades. But as growth rates stall, companies in China for China, Chinese exporters, those with international ambitions, and multinational companies in, and coming into China have a new challenge on their hands. How do they run a profitable business today, while gearing up for future innovation in a world of increasing geopolitical, economic and social uncertainty?
GenAI offers the potential to boost efficiency, automate production, leverage the shrinking workforce in effective ways and speed up scientific discoveries. Chinese GenAI is here to stay. But will China’s industries catch up quick enough to create the next comparative advantage? This is too early to say. What is clear is that China can no longer rely on cheap labour or manufacturing prowess (still No 1 in the world!), and even the innovation advantage is becoming increasingly contingent on the application of AI, and continued access to the latest technologies.

title: ‘Shadow AI’: The Controversial 2024 Trend That Could Create Disaster, Experts Say
text:
The term “Shadow AI” has over 281,000 Google results The reason why the term is blowing up now? Nearly half (45%) of executives have adopted a “wait and watch” approach to AI adoption, but employees are missing the memo with 75% using AI at work. That practice is known as “Shadow AI,” and it’s a potential disaster that can cause havoc within an organization, according to Sreekanth Menon, Genpact's global head of AI/ML. He built Genpact’s AI practice from the ground up back in 2017. Genpact is an AI-first $4.5B professional services firm deploying and continually refining AI strategies with the world’s most powerful and largest companies.
What Is ‘Shadow AI?’
I spoke by email with Menon, who told me that “Shadow AI” is the use of AI by employees within an organization without the necessary approvals and/or oversight. He informed me that there are many uses of the technology that remain unsanctioned by leadership, IT and security teams and use of ChatGPT 0utside company servers and IT systems.
Why Is This Happening?
“With the rapid advancements in generative AI, the workforce has found consumer-grade AI tools, like ChatGPT, readily accessible and useful for tasks such as writing, designing and coding, Menon states. He cites that Over 50% of US employees already incorporate AI tools in their work, often without formal approval because of the lack of organizational policies and slow IT approval processes.
I wrote a piece for Forbes.com on “Shadow IT” earlier this year. “Shadow IT” is the use of an unapproved tool to access, store or share corporate data or when an employee accesses an approved tool in an unauthorized way. The recent explosive popularity of generative AI applications like ChatGPT have led to a rise in shadow AI, which is the unsanctioned use of artificial intelligence.
I asked Menon about the difference between “Shadow AI” and “Shadow IT.” He explains that “Shadow AI” has evolved from “Shadow IT,” which has been a long-standing problem across organizations. “For example, employees leveraging personal mobile devices for business needs. With more employees experimenting with AI in both personal and professional settings, and the technology transforming the corporate landscape, it’s important for organizations of all sizes to understand the risks associated with it.”
What Are The Implications For Employers/Employees
According to Menon, “Unsanctioned AI use can result in non-compliance with regulations, such as the EU AI Act, risking significant fines and penalties.” He notes that employees may unintentionally expose sensitive data to AI tools that lack proper security measures, adding that, “This could lead to data breaches, non-compliance with regulations like GDPR and potential legal repercussions. AI tools not vetted by IT can introduce vulnerabilities, including prompt injections and training data poisoning, potentially compromising the organization's cybersecurity.”
Menon acknowledges that “Shadow IT” and “Shadow AI” are by-in-large unavoidable, more so in the context of GenAI. “This is because adoption cycles are faster with LLM-based applications,” he explains. “The threshold of accessibility is lower compared to cloud technologies or traditional AI in general where one required to have some amount of using IDEs or coding knowledge. Faster adoption cycles condense decision making cycles in an enterprise, which makes it challenging for the CIOs and CISOs to frame appropriate risk mitigation strategies.”
I asked Menon what employers can do to mitigate this risk. He informed me of the importance that employers understand that the unsanctioned use of AI could have disastrous consequences, such as security breaches, unfair advantages across an employee base and legal issues/liability concerns. “It’s paramount that organizations set cohesive policies and align on how AI is being leveraged across departments,” he insists. “In addition to alignment, there needs to be more awareness spread throughout the organization, beyond just security teams, about the risks of AI. It’s essential for CIOs to be more proactive about explaining these risks and spreading awareness. For instance, encouraging employees to report unsanctioned use of LLM-based applications. Transparency helps in identifying the threat vectors in such a fast changing landscape and avoid risks.”

title: Global Competition Scrutiny Gains Traction With AI Leaders
text:
Over the last several weeks, we’ve seen Microsoft and Apple drop their involvement in OpenAI’s Board, and subsequently, the leaders of the US, UK and EU competition authorities made clear that their scrutiny of AI will endure. Specifically, while those authorities see great economic potential in AI, they also see potential for consumer and business harm if AI does not experience vibrant competition.
Microsoft invested $13 billion in OpenAI, and had an observer role on OpenAI’s Board until it announced its intention to withdraw from that role. Apple had also expected to take a similar role on the Board, but OpenAI said it would not be taking on Board observers after Microsoft’s departure.
Industry observers believe this change was, at least in part, due to FTC, DOJ, and EU scrutiny of AI leaders. The scrutiny centers on the purported undue influence that existing market leaders could have on the development of AI use cases and potentially tilt the competitive playing field in favor of those investors.
These concerns were first reported in DOJ’s announcement of its investigation into Nvidia and FTC’s concurrent investigation into Microsoft and OpenAI. While there is certainly debate over whether the government’s concerns are well-grounded, the fact remains that the concerns may be driving behavior from the firms.
Most recently, the FTC, DOJ, UK’s Competition Markets Authority (CMA), and the EU issued a joint statement confirming that while each of their authority remains sovereign and independent, they have specific concerns regarding: (i) concentrated control of key inputs, (ii) the use of economic power in certain parts of the AI stack to disrupt future innovation, and (iii) deals between AI firms that allegedly can enrich themselves to the detriment of the public.
These concerns echo those set out in President Biden’s October 2023 Executive Order regarding the “Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence.” The Executive Order directs the Department of Commerce and National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop safety and security standards for the development of AI, including the sharing of testing results for safety.
Similarly, the Executive Order called on Congress to pass bipartisan data privacy legislation, and encourages agencies to innovate in the collection of information to strengthen privacy governance. As with the President’s July 2021 Executive Order on Competition, it directed the FTC to engage in rulemaking around the use of AI.
While AI is still in its relative infancy, lawmakers, regulators and antitrust enforcers are currently using available tools to study the development of this technology and to determine who stands to gain the most from each significant development. Put another way, the government is using the consumer protection, antitrust, and even labor angles (for jobs that may be replaced by AI) to ensure that the advancement of AI does not come at too great a societal cost.
Leadership Strategy Implications
A company’s relationship with AI may take on one or more roles, but fundamentally, it appears that at least four of those roles are: (i) “developer,” or companies that are developing or innovating different layers of the AI stack, (ii) “business partner,” or those providing resources and/or know-how in bringing AI to market, (iii) “data sources” being used for the development of AI, and (iv) users, either for business or personal purposes.
It is clear that the government’s efforts are focused on protecting the latter two categories (data sources and users), and looking at the first two groups (developers and business partners) as parties to be potentially scrutinized for negative outcomes.
Thus, it is critical that companies in either the developer and/or business partner roles can easily and persuasively explain how each of their actions or initiatives are benefitting users and not sacrificing the interests of users or data sources. Similarly, consistent with the overall approach of this administration (see prior article on President Biden’s Prior Executive Order on Competition), the government will be looking for interested parties to submit input and comments on how the competitive process is developing.
Such interested parties could include any type of data source or user, and as a result, developers and business partners should be sensitive to the claims being made by those groups, even if they sharply disagree with them. A well-conceived communications and PR strategy that addresses users is likely to be worth the investment.
While the uses of AI have greatly expanded in recent years, future uses that could fundamentally change the economy or even a specific industry sector are where enforcers are likely seeking to preserve competition. To that end, companies would be best served to explain how they are contributing to future advancements of AI for the benefit of the public.
Thus, in any business negotiation or development effort regarding AI, the concepts articulated by global enforcers should be well-considered and discussed. To that end, any effort to hinder the government’s understanding of AI will likely be received with suspicion.
In the end, AI represents a great opportunity for many companies, and those companies must be cognizant of the role government will play in its development.

title: Council Post: The AI Maturity Model And Its Impact On Marketing
text:
Alex Kudos has over 20 years experience in marketing and currently serves as CMO at Social Discovery Group.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is more than just a tech trend—it’s a transformative force that has altered the landscape of modern marketing. The integration of AI into marketing has flipped the industry upside down, and companies need to adapt to maintain their positions.
Incorporating AI into a marketing strategy can best be executed by following the steps of the AI Maturity Model, a framework that is used to assess and evaluate the level of maturity of an area within an organization. This model can help organizations enhance their AI capabilities systematically, understand the steps required to improve their processes and establish a road map for achieving their goals. To evaluate our stage with AI, Social Discovery Group followed this model, which transformed our company and helped us incorporate AI into everyday operations.
Understanding The Five Levels Of AI Maturity
1. Awareness: Companies have minimal knowledge about AI and are not using it but are curious about its potential impact.
2. Active Phase: Companies start using AI in specific areas like data science and analytics.
3. Operational Phase: Companies optimize processes and employ AI tools more broadly.
4. Systematic Phase: Companies build new business models and tools to improve efficiency and innovation.
5. Transformational Phase: AI becomes part of the business’s DNA, exemplified by companies like Amazon and Google.
Social Discovery Group currently sits in level four but is on the verge of reaching level five, where it is being implemented across our company. We have built our own tools to improve efficiency and are continuously being innovative to make our business grow and help ensure our users have exceptional experiences.
It may be daunting to understand where a brand or business falls in its AI maturity, but once it is determined, here are the stages of the model to begin to implement.
Transitioning Through The Stages
Phase 1: Analyze
Evaluate current AI capabilities by conducting a comprehensive audit of marketing processes to identify gaps and opportunities. This sets the foundation for AI integration.
Phase 2: Plan
This phase is about developing a strategic approach to AI integration. Companies can start by identifying AI applications within their marketing operations. These might include chatbots for customer service, AI-driven content creation or machine learning algorithms for targeted advertising.
The planning phase involves prioritizing these AI initiatives based on their potential impact and feasibility. This ensures that resources are allocated efficiently and efforts are focused on high-impact projects. A well-defined road map is created, aligning AI initiatives with broader business objectives. This structured approach is essential for ensuring that AI integration is both strategic and scalable.
Phase 3: Experiment
With a clear plan in place, the next step is to experiment. This is where AI tools and technologies are deployed across various marketing functions. The focus here is on leveraging the AI strategy to drive efficiency, enhance productivity and improve business performance. During the experimentation phase, companies might pilot AI-driven campaigns, test automated content generation or deploy AI-powered customer segmentation models. This phase is ongoing, with continuous testing and refinement to ensure that AI initiatives deliver the desired outcomes.
Phase 4: Evaluate
Measure and optimize AI initiatives' performance by monitoring KPIs and using data to assess effectiveness. Refine strategies based on insights to ensure AI solutions evolve with changing business needs and market conditions.
Phase 5: Innovate
Foster a culture of innovation and experimentation. In this phase, organizations might invest in cutting-edge AI research, explore novel AI applications or partner with AI startups to stay at the forefront of technological advancements. By embracing a forward-thinking mindset, companies can identify untapped business potential and pioneering solutions that set them apart from competitors. Innovation is key to sustaining growth and staying ahead in the rapidly evolving AI landscape.
By following the AI Maturity Model, companies can systematically integrate AI into their marketing strategies and harness its full potential. This structured approach helps ensure that AI initiatives are strategic, impactful and continuously evolving, enabling organizations to stay competitive and achieve sustained success in the age of AI-driven marketing.

title: Council Post: Growth Of AI In Programmatic: Just A Trend Or Must-Have?
text:
Roman Vrublivskyi is the experienced CEO of SmartHub, a global ad tech company that provides white-label programmatic solutions.
Artificial intelligence is conquering the entire ecosystem of digital advertising, and programmatic isn’t an exception. The majority of marketers are already leveraging AI-powered tools in programmatic advertising or plan to start using them in the near future, while only 5% have no such plans. Due to enhanced personalization, optimized bidding, predictive analytics and targeting capabilities in the coming cookieless era, AI leaves virtually no one indifferent.
However, the programmatic industry is continuously evolving, with new trends emerging and fading away regularly. So, is AI just another trend or a must-have technology?
The Role Of AI In Programmatic Advertising
Programmatic advertising is pretty smart on its own since it automates the ad buying and selling process. However, AI makes it even smarter, enabling advertisers to reach their potential customers with higher accuracy and, as a result, drive conversions.
And improved targeting isn’t the only advantage. AI automates or streamlines multiple tasks, starting with generating creative copy for an ad and ending with forecasting trends. Here are just a couple of its benefits and applications in programmatic advertising.
• More precise targeting thanks to AI’s capability to examine user behavior with higher effectiveness. This way, the ads’ ROI increases.
• Cost-efficiency since the number of wasted impressions is reduced and the budget is allocated more appropriately.
• Dynamic creative optimization ensures incredible personalization and allows marketers to deliver the right ads to the right users at the right time.
• Identifying patterns in the vast array of data (including first-party data) allows for making data-driven decisions faster and more effectively.
• Predictive analytics enables advertisers to detect opportunities and react on time.
• Content generation for ad creatives (copy, visuals, etc.).
• Fraud detection capabilities ensure only genuine traffic.
Who Can Benefit From AI The Most?
Marketers are obviously the main category benefiting from using AI in programmatic advertising, but they are not the only ones. Actually, leveraging AI brings value to all the parties involved.
For instance, more accurate targeting and dynamic creative optimization ensure more relevant advertising experiences for potential customers, which is beneficial for publishers since their traffic won’t be affected. Additionally, AI helps website and app owners sell their ad inventory at optimal prices and maximize revenue.
As for the owners of programmatic platforms, enhancing their solutions with AI capabilities enables them to remain competitive and drive income. Since more and more marketers are starting to use AI, integrating such functionalities becomes a must.
Is AI A Trend Or A Must-Have?
Considering the above-mentioned benefits, as well as the increasing number of AI adopters in the programmatic industry, artificial intelligence is definitely a must-have piece of technology. Using AI-powered tools and programmatic platforms is a way to automate routine tasks, streamline processes, enhance advertising strategies and remain competitive in the modern market.
For those willing to implement AI in programmatic advertising, the following steps are crucial to take.
• Invest in data infrastructure. AI heavily relies on data, so it is essential to ensure its high quality and robust infrastructure. The data should comply with standards like GDPR and be secured. Sharing sensitive data with tools like ChatGPT must be avoided—as such, software can then leverage this data in other responses.
• Select a programmatic platform. There are multiple options available, but it is important to choose one that will align with your goals and enable you to access the required ad formats and environments. Look for a platform with advanced targeting and analytics capabilities, and thoroughly explore other features before making a choice. After this, educate your team on using the solution.
• Analyze the performance continuously. In programmatic advertising, AI is a powerful ally, but it is still crucial to monitor the performance of ad campaigns to detect weaknesses and opportunities. The human touch still remains a key component for the success of ad campaigns.
• Invest in additional AI tools. Apart from a programmatic platform, it would be wise to implement AI solutions for data analysis as the detected patterns and predicted trends enable data-driven decision making. Look for applications that comply with data regulations and are transparent regarding how the data is used.
AI Is Not The Future Of Programmatic Advertising — It's Here Today
Nowadays, AI is often called the future of advertising, including the programmatic model. However, it is essential to understand that AI isn’t only about the future—it is about the present. It has quickly turned from a trend into a must-have technology that reshapes the entire advertising industry, and we can expect even more applications to enter the stage. AI is already here, and it is not going anywhere.
Yes, it has always been associated with concerns about job displacement, but in my opinion, these fears are not grounded enough. For instance, AI can analyze vast amounts of data promptly and summarize the key outcomes, but the human element is required to make a decision regarding advertising strategy. AI lacks human creativity, intuition and the ability to understand specific nuances of the market or audience. Additionally, AI tools still require someone to operate them, which means there is a demand for professionals with the necessary skills.
Those businesses that haven’t started implementing AI in their programmatic strategies yet are already falling behind, as being competitive in the modern market implies leveraging AI’s power to be faster and more efficient. There is no time to hesitate—such organizations need to adopt this technology as soon as possible and upskill their employees. Additionally, it is essential to keep an eye on the evolution of AI. The technology is still developing, and monitoring its progress is another activity required to maintain a competitive advantage.

title: Instructure Canvas Weaving AI Throughout The Educational Fabric
text:
Canvas, the ubiquitous learning management system from Instructure, is well positioned at the center of the AI transformation of education. At InstructureCon 2024, an event featuring over 3,000 attendees and 500 employees, I spoke with Mitch Benson, Instructure’s Chief Strategy Officer, who had announced the release of over 200 AI-related innovations, partnerships, and product enhancements focused on educational effectiveness and the learner journey. These AI tools will be freely available to Canvas customers, constituting tens of millions of educators across over 7,000 organizations.
While expansive in reach, Instructure has taken a measured approach to deploying AI, wanting to ensure that any tool deployed satisfies primary educational objectives, preserves safety and data privacy, and brings identifiable benefits to students and instructors. AI needs to do more than just generate content; it needs to improve the underlying learning.
The Emerging AI Marketplace showcases products and services that work seamlessly within Canvas. All products come with an “AI nutrition fact” label that provides transparency into LLMs and data policies, helping institutions keep AI within policy. Featured tools include discussion summaries for complex discussion threads, summaries of inbox messages, and semantic search tools—tools helping students and educators cut through the proliferation of information help with navigation are becoming essential counterparts to the rapid deployment of generative AI.
AI Supporting Education Beyond Content Generation
When evaluating AI in education, the question that must be asked is “how is it improving education?” Is it scaling quality? Is it driving efficiency? Is it keeping the teacher-centered in the instructional process, deepening relationships with students, or displacing the teacher?
Mitch Benson gave the example of assessing student papers. The better the paper production tools afforded to students, the longer the papers become. Is the best use of teacher time to read everything the student writes? Or should it focus on providing high-value comments to sections of the writing? Or should the teacher focus on areas where the student falls short and provide the guidance needed to improve?
The answers will ultimately depend on the nature of the assignment and what is being taught. If it is a class where the goal is teaching students how to write formal essays, an AI can likely do as good a job as a teacher in doing a preliminary read-through. Suppose it is a stack of term papers on distinct subjects, such as one might have in an upper-division philosophy course, where the focus is on argumentation. In that case, it will remain incumbent on the instructor to do the reading as the learning will come less from the writing of the paper as it will from the subsequent arguing over the points made in the paper.
Shifting From Static Objects To Dynamic Processes
Where AI can change the game in teaching, especially within a learning management system, is in its ability to shift the focus from student work product to student work process. Traditionally, papers are static, the results of a writing process. Using papers as teaching tools is challenging. An instructor can fill a page with comments, but unless a student can reconstruct their headspace from the moment they did the writing, the comments may fall flat. An AI deployed as an attentive teaching assistant can gain insight into the student’s work process and intervene appropriately to address mistakes as they are being made, which is the optimal teaching moment. AI can also develop a working model of the student and the standard progression of students from novice to expert as they go through a course. The AI can use this model to ensure that the comments given focus on the areas of expected difficulty and maximum potential growth.
Beyond Courses And Degrees
As more becomes known about individuals more and more data about learner journeys and the alignment of courses to skills and skills to careers, Instructure will become increasingly capable of providing optimal pathways for students. Moreover, by combining learning management system, student work repository, transcripts, and credentialling services through the integration of products such as Portfolium, Parchment, Scribbles, and Concentric Sky, Instructure will be able to provide students and prospective employers with deep longitudinal insight into capabilities and qualifications. Rather than just being able to provide information about course outcomes, as with the traditional transcript, Insturcture could make available the entire student data set leading to that outcome. This would make it possible to distinguish between the student earning a “B” in a course who started rough but was a solid “A” for the last month of the course, and the “B” student who started strong but grew progressively weaker as the course progressed. One struggles to diferentiate between such students when reviewing traditional academic records, but it will become clear as more data is available.
As the data set grows, developing AI-enhanced interfaces into the data will become increasingly important to help viewers find precisely what they are looking for. One can easily imagine a world where the degrees become less valuable than the incremental steps recorded en route to the degree. This would move the ultimate stamp of approval on the finished product (students) from the supplier’s (university) quality control staff (faculty, registrar) to that of the buyer (potential employer), who could use the AI to make find exactly what they are looking for independent of the grades assigned. As this happens, students may find themselves with many more choices on how to meet a prospective employer’s requirements than simply going to a name-brand university and majoring in a pre-approved subject. The ultimate democratization of education may reside not in its universal availability but in its deinstitutionalization. If this comes to pass, we may find that the fabric of our lives is Canvas.
